During the review process, the reviewers raise some concerns regarding the preference of phase modeling over learned motion space diffusion alone, the lack of comparisons with more recent baseline methods, the evaluation metrics, the use of a simple linear blending step for final smoothing, motion transition, etc. Most of these issues were adequately addressed in the rebuttal and acknowledged by the reviewers. Ultimately, this paper received uniformly positive scores, and all reviewers recommend its acceptance in light of the significance of the research direction and the strength of its contributions.

The ACs consider the generation of compositional and transitional motions to be a key area of research. Specifically, the proposed Compositional Phase Diffusion framework introduces a scalable and novel approach to long-term compositional motion generation that improves transitions, outperforms state-of-the-art methods in motion realism and contextual alignment, and demonstrates consistent advantages across multiple motion synthesis tasks. The framework’s decoupled SPDM and TPDM modules reduce task interference and, together with parallel processing of multiple motion segments, enable flexible sequencing and smoother, semantically consistent transitions compared to hard-coded methods. Considering the strength of its contributions, the AC recommends acceptance as an oral presentation. The decision was discussed and confirmed with the SAC.

Authors should incorporate the feedback into the final version, and include comparisons with general text-to-motion methods to demonstrate how additional annotations can contribute to addressing the broader text-to-motion task.

Thank you for your thoughtful comments. We will thoughtfully address all of your suggestions and concerns in our revised submission.

> [Weakness 1] The authors do not convincingly explain why phase modeling should be preferred over learned motion space diffusion alone. While the method builds upon PAE and related works, the motivation for combining phase modeling could be better justified, particularly in contrast to simpler raw motion diffusion modeling or VAE-based methods.

We evaluated our method against PCMDM and PriorMDM, which are established baselines for learned motion space diffusion, as well as MLD, a representative VAE-based approach for motion generation, given the lack of more recent VAE-based methods for long-term motion generation. Notably, our SPDM (Sec 3.1.2) and TPDM (Sec 3.1.3) architectures require both param-level tokens (F,A,B,S) and frame-level tokens (Q), available only in phase-modeled space, making direct adaptation to motion space diffusion or VAE-based frameworks challenging. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms these baselines, indicating that phase modeling achieves superior performance over motion space diffusion in both compositional generation and motion inbetweening tasks.
Furthermore, the motivation for employing phase modeling instead of raw motion diffusion is discussed in the Introduction (Sec. 1), specifically the need to capture the intrinsic kinematics of each segment to enable smooth transitions. We acknowledge that our previous description was unclear, as it referenced PriorMDM and our method without explicitly distinguishing between raw motion diffusion and phase modeling. We will revise the manuscript to enhance clarity on this point.

> [Weakness 2] The paper lacks comparisons with more recent baseline methods, such as FlowMDM[1], which may offer stronger performance or complementary insights, especially in long-term motion generation and transition quality.

In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we performed additional experiments using FlowMDM. Due to the limited time available during the rebuttal period, we utilized the publicly provided model weights and inference pipeline to adapt FlowMDM for the compositional motion pair generation task. The results, presented in the table below, demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to FlowMDM. Note that PCCAT in FlowMDM is trained to learn semantic alignment directly on pairs of subsequences, having significantly increased training complexity and a more complicated inference pipeline compared to our SPDM approach, where alignment is learned on individual subsequences.

| Compositional Motion Pair Generation  \| | Smt FID ↓ | Trn FID ↓ | Overall FID ↓ | Smt MMD ↓ | Trn MMD ↓ | Overall MMD ↓ |
| ---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| FlowMDM  \| | 1.619 | 7.978 | 4.102 | 7.695 | 7.674 | 7.031|
| Ours  \| | **0.736** | **1.807** | **0.782** | **3.509** | **6.545** | **4.711** |

> [Weakness 3] Despite emphasis on the proposed framework's parallel denoising capability and scalability, the paper does not provide any empirical analysis on inference efficiency or generation latency.

We observed that the original description provides only limited information regarding parallelism, which makes it challenging to clearly understand the generation time and inference efficiency. To clarify this, we will add the following empirical analysis to the supplementary materials:
We empirically measured inference time for long-term motion generation. For scenarios with 2 subsequences, the total inference time is approximately 1.705 seconds, while for 10 subsequences, it is about 2.015 seconds. The SPDM and TPDM models require approximately 0.010 and 0.015 seconds per inference, respectively. Since subsequences are stacked along the batch dimension and processed in parallel by SPDM and TPDM, the model inference time per loop remains around 0.015 seconds, independent of the number of subsequences. In contrast, the phase mixing and rearrangement of the inferred subsequences require 0.002 seconds for 2 subsequences and 0.005 seconds for 10 subsequences.
After 100 diffusion loops, the total diffusion stage takes roughly 1.7 seconds for 2 subsequences and 2.0 seconds for 10 subsequences. For the final motion decoding step, decoding times are 0.005 seconds for 2 subsequences and 0.015 seconds for 14 subsequences. In contrast to SPDM and TPDM inference, the subsequence rearrangement and linear blending steps do scale with the number of subsequences, as linear blending across overlapping regions cannot be efficiently parallelized.

> [Weakness 4] The user study relies on feedback from only 11 judges, which constitutes a rather limited sample size and raises concerns about the statistical reliability and potential bias in the subjective evaluation results.

To enhance statistical reliability, we expanded the user study by recruiting an additional 19 judges during the rebuttal period, resulting in a total of 30 participants. The updated user study results, shown on the right side of the table below, are consistent with our previous findings.

Thanks for your constructive feedback. We carefully consider your comments and address your concerns in our response.

> [Question 1] Please provide an ablation study evaluating performance without the final linear blending step. Given that the core of your method is designed to ensure phase continuity, is this blending still a critical component for hiding artifacts, or is it more of a final polish?

Linear blending is employed to combine the transitioning segment generated by TPDM with the semantic-conditioned segments from SPDM within the overlapping region. However, since the semantic-conditioned segments in our setup do not overlap, linear blending cannot be applied, resulting in motion discontinuity artifacts such as sudden jumps. Therefore, incorporating linear blending with the transition segment is crucial for eliminating abrupt transitions between motion segments.
The ablation results without linear blending are shown in the table below. The presence of motion discontinuity artifacts leads to an increase in Trn FID. Furthermore, the absence of linear blending causes a slight decrease in Smt FID, while Smt MMD remains largely unchanged. These observations are consistent with results from priorMDM studies with reduced transition lengths, where transitional segments are generated by machine learning models rather than hard-coded signal processing methods, as detailed in Supplementary Table 7.

| compositional motion pair generation  \| | Smt FID ↓ | Trn FID ↓ | Overall FID ↓ | Smt MMD ↓ | Trn MMD ↓ | Overall MMD ↓ |
| ---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| w/o linear blend  \| | **0.729** | 2.295 | 1.061 | 3.570 | **5.782** | 4.970 |
| Ours  \| | 0.736 | **1.807** | **0.782** | **3.509** | 6.545 | **4.711** |

> [Question 2] The transition motion $X_t$ is defined as covering the second half of $X_p$ and the first half of $X_s$, This seems intuitive when they have similar lengths. How is this handled when their lengths are highly dissimilar (e.g., a 2-second action followed by a 8-second action)? Or is there a upper limit for the time window?

The transition motion $X_t$ covers the second half of $X_p$ and the first half of $X_s$, even when their lengths diﬀer signiﬁcantly. For example, if $X_p$ is 2 seconds and $X_s$ is 8 seconds, $X_t$ will span 5 seconds, covering the last 1 second of $X_p$ and the ﬁrst 4 seconds of $X_s$. Note that the maximum length of $X_t$ remains 8 seconds (the same as maximum motion length), which occurs when both $X_p$ and $X_s$ are 8 seconds long.

Thank you for your constructive feedback. We will provide detailed responses to your questions.

> [Weakness 1] Justification and Generalizability of the Phase Representation: A core premise of the framework is that a periodic phase representation is universally superior for human motion. However, a large number of human actions are inherently non-cyclic and transient. Whether this method has optimal generalizability for all types of motion is a question worth exploring.

We would like to clarify the core assumption of our framework. Our approach is based on the use of periodic phase representation to improve the smoothness of transitions between generated motion segments, rather than claiming universal superiority in modeling human motion. The concern regarding modeling different motion segments with periodic phase representation is analogous to the use of FFT in image space, where even aperiodic signals can be represented as combinations of phase signals across various frequency bands. Moreover, in our framework, the distribution of frequency in the phase channels is learned rather than fixed, as in FFT, which provides greater flexibility for modeling aperiodic signals. A remaining challenge of the periodic phase representation is accurately modeling subtle motion patterns, such as minor movements related to body balance or object contact, which contribute minimally to the reconstruction loss during ACT-PAE training. This limitation, due to reduced expressiveness, is discussed in the Limitation section (Supplementary Section 5).

> [Weakness 2] Potential for Error Propagation: The quality of the final output is critically dependent on the fidelity of the initial ACT-PAE encoding. The ACT-PAE is trained by the reconstruction loss. However, reconstructing the motion well does not guarantee that the resulting latent phase space is optimal for the downstream diffusion task. The authors should discuss this in the revison.

Regarding the issue of error propagation, our experiments presented in the main paper demonstrate that our model outperforms other approaches, including those based on raw motion diffusion modeling (e.g., PCMDM, PriorMDM) as well as VAE-based methods (e.g., MLD). All experiments were conducted within the context of downstream diffusion tasks, such as Compositional Motion Pair Generation, Long-term Motion Generation, and Motion Inbetweening. The results consistently highlight the advantages of ACT-PAE encoding in these scenarios.

> [Question 1] The ACT-PAE is the cornerstone of the entire framework. How does it perform on highly aperiodic, non-cyclic motions (e.g., stumbling, complex object interaction, modern dance)? Have you quantified its reconstruction error on such motions and compared it with more standard VAE-based autoencoders?

Regarding concerns about reconstruction error between the VAE and our proposed ACT-PAE, we observe that while the VAE achieves lower reconstruction error during training, its reconstruction error is higher during testing. Our experimental results further indicate that the testing reconstruction error of the encoding method shows a stronger correlation with performance on downstream diffusion tasks than the training reconstruction error.

Thank you for your valuable feedback. We will address the concerns regarding the identified weaknesses and respond to your questions accordingly.

> [Weaknesses 1] The paper relies on the BABEL-TEACH dataset for training and evaluation, which may limit the generalizability of the proposed method. The authors acknowledge that BABEL-TEACH is the only dataset providing subsequence pair annotations, but this could restrict the applicability of the framework to other motion datasets.

This weakness is addressed in Supplementary Section 5.2. We believe that developing datasets of subsequence motion pairs annotated across different modalities could further expand the potential applications of our approach.

>  [Weaknesses 2] The paper proposes a phase mixing parameter r to balance semantic denoising and transitional denoising, but it does not thoroughly explore the impact of different r values on motion quality and transition smoothness. A more comprehensive ablation study on this parameter would strengthen the paper.

Ablation studies on different phase mixing parameters are provided in Supplementary Section 3.5. The impact of these parameters on motion quality is presented using the FID metric in Supplementary Table 5, while their influence on transition smoothness is evaluated using the RMS-Jerk and NPSS metrics in Supplementary Table 6. 

>  [Weaknesses 3] The paper primarily uses FID and MMD for evaluation, but these metrics may not fully capture the nuances of motion quality, particularly aspects like motion dynamics and physical plausibility. Incorporating additional metrics, such as joint velocity errors or root mean squared jerk, could provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

We would like to clarify that root mean squared jerk (RMS-Jerk) has been included as an evaluation metric for the Motion Inbetweening experiment, as reported in both the main paper and the supplementary materials.

>  [Questions 1] How would the proposed framework perform on other motion datasets, such as HumanML3D or AMASS? Are there any dataset-specific factors that might affect the framework's performance? How are the performances compared to recent motion generation methods like MoMask?

Our proposed framework requires datasets with subsequence pair annotations for training, which are not available in HumanML3D and AMASS. Consequently, all comparative evaluations are conducted solely on the BABEL-TEACH dataset, which limits our ability to explore dataset-specific factors. 
Regarding text-based long motion generation methods such as MoMask, their application and experimental settings differ significantly from ours. Notably, MoMask does not allow for specification of motion duration for individual segments, whereas our framework requires each conditioned segment to have a specified duration. This fundamental difference renders direct comparison infeasible and potentially unfair. Therefore, these text-based long motion generation methods are not included in our experimental comparisons.

> [Questions 2] The paper proposes a phase mixing parameter r to balance semantic denoising and transitional denoising, but it does not thoroughly explore the impact of different r values on motion quality and transition smoothness. A more comprehensive ablation study on this parameter would strengthen the paper.

The phase mixing parameters were selected based on the ablation study presented in Supplementary Section 3.5. Although these parameters are fixed during inference in our current framework, it is possible that introducing learnable parameters or an adaptive mechanism could further enhance performance. However, implementing such features would likely require an additional training stage and a more complex inference pipeline, which is beyond the scope of this work. We plan to add a paragraph in the future work section to discuss this potential direction. 

> [Questions 3] The motion inbetweening experiments focus on relatively short transition lengths (60-180 frames). How would the framework perform for longer inbetweening tasks, such as generating transitions spanning several seconds or more?

The duration of the inbetweening segment in the motion inbetweening experiment is determined by the minimum and maximum motion lengths set during the training process. For reference, 180 frames at 30 FPS corresponds to 6 seconds, which is already considered a long segment. While it is technically feasible to generate longer inbetweening segments, the testing dataset contains few sequences exceeding 180 frames, making evaluations for longer segments statistically unreliable (e.g., the FID metric returns NaN for the CMIB experiment at 240 frames).

summary.value: In this paper, the authors propose Compositional Phase Diffusion, a framework for generating long, semantically coherent motion sequences with smooth transitions. The method introduces Semantic Phase Diffusion Module (SPDM) and Transitional Phase Diffusion Module (TPDM)—which operate within a latent phase space learned by a transformer-based Action-Centric Periodic Autoencoder (ACT-PAE). By encoding motions as periodic signals, the framework enables semantically guided denoising and dynamic coherence between motion segments. SPDM integrates text-conditioned semantics, while TPDM ensures smooth transitions by diffusing phase dynamics from neighboring segments. The framework supports parallel processing of variable-length motion clips, allowing for scalable compositional motion generation and motion inbetweening. Experiments on the BABEL-TEACH dataset demonstrate state of art performance in long motion generation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
#### **Strengths**

1. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple tasks, including Compositional Motion Pair Generation, Long-term Motion Generation, and Unconditional Motion In-between.
2. The authors conduct comprehensive ablation studies that effectively validate the design and effectiveness of the proposed architecture.

#### **Weaknesses**

1. The authors do not convincingly explain why phase modeling should be preferred over learned motion space diffusion alone. While the method builds upon PAE and related works, the motivation for combining phase modeling could be better justified, particularly in contrast to simpler raw motion diffusion modeling or VAE-based methods.
2. The paper lacks comparisons with more recent baseline methods, such as FlowMDM[1], which may offer stronger performance or complementary insights, especially in long-term motion generation and transition quality.
3. Despite emphasis on the proposed framework's parallel denoising capability and scalability, the paper does not provide any empirical analysis on inference efficiency or generation latency.
4. The user study relies on feedback from only 11 judges, which constitutes a rather limited sample size and raises concerns about the statistical reliability and potential bias in the subjective evaluation results.

#### Minor
1. Line#100: The notation $mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{F}, \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{S}]$ is introduced without sufficient explanation or definition.
2. The notation $\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{tf}}$ used in the caption of Figure 2 is inconsistent with that in line#156.

summary.value:
This paper introduces "Compositional Phase Diffusion," a novel framework for generating long, composite 3D human motions from a series of text prompts. The core contribution is a method for creating smooth, kinematically plausible transitions between different motion segments, a common failure point for existing models. The framework operates in a learned latent phase space designed to capture the periodic dynamics of human motion. It consists of three main components: 

1. An Action-Centric Periodic Autoencoder that encodes variable-length motions into a unified phase representation
2. A Semantic Phase Diffusion Module for text-conditional generation
3. A Transitional Phase Diffusion Module, which is the key innovation. The TPDM ensures smooth transitions by having adjacent motion clips mutually influence each other's dynamics throughout the parallel diffusion process.

The authors demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on compositional generation and motion inbetweening tasks on the BABEL-TEACH dataset.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strengths

1. The core idea of performing motion composition via diffusion in a learned phase space is noval. The TPDM module, which co-generates and dynamically aligns adjacent clips, is a more principled approach to creating smooth transitions than the post-hoc blending techniques used by prior work.

2. The framework is technically sound. The ACT-PAE is a well-motivated Transformer-based improvement over prior convolutional phase autoencoders, enabling the use of variable-length motion clips.

3. The paper is well-written and clearly structured.

# Weaknesses

1. The framework's complexity is a minor drawback. It consists of three separately trained transformer models (ACT-PAE, SPDM, TPDM), the inference time (~2s per subsequence pair) is acceptable, but not fast.

2. The pipeline concludes with a simple linear blending step to smooth the final decoded segments, which raises questions about the TPDM's effectiveness. If the phase-space alignment were successful, this step should be unnecessary. I would like to know "how bad" the results will be without it.

questions.value:
1. Please provide an ablation study evaluating performance without the final linear blending step. Given that the core of your method is designed to ensure phase continuity, is this blending still a critical component for hiding artifacts, or is it more of a final polish?

2. The transition motion $X_t$ is defined as covering the second half of $X_p$ and the first half of $X_s$, This seems intuitive when they have similar lengths. How is this handled when their lengths are highly dissimilar (e.g., a 2-second action followed by a 8-second action)? Or is there a upper limit for the time window?

summary.value: This paper introduces a novel framework named "Deep Compositional Phase Diffusion" to address the challenge of creating long motion sequences with different types of actions, while ensuring the transitions between them are not only smooth but also dynamically plausible and semantically coherent. This work proposes a two-stage alternating framework to solve this problem. It decomposes the motion generation process into two sub-tasks: 1) semantic content generation, and 2) transitional motion modeling, and proposes two modules, the Semantic Phase Diffusion Module (SPDM) and Transitional Phase Diffusion Module (TPDM) to solve these two tasks. Moreover, this work also shifts the diffusion process from the traditional kinematic data space to a learned "phase latent space" using the pre-trained Action-Centric Motion Phase Autoencoder (ACT-PAE).

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The Phase-Space Diffusion Paradigm: This method uses ACT-PAE to decompose motion into parameters describing its core dynamics (frequency, amplitude, etc.), which is similar to the field of signal processing, transforming a time-domain signal to the frequency domain. The use of ACT-PAE allows the subsequent diffusion modules (SPDM and TPDM) to learn on a more abstract and semantically meaningful representation.
2. Decoupled Control: The design of the explicit separation of the tasks of semantic content generation (handled by SPDM) and transitional continuity assurance (handled by TPDM) is another strength. By assigning these two goals to specialized modules, the framework effectively mitigates interference between tasks, allowing each module to be optimized for its specific objective.

Weaknesses:
1. Justification and Generalizability of the Phase Representation: A core premise of the framework is that a periodic phase representation is universally superior for human motion. However, a large number of human actions are inherently non-cyclic and transient. Whether this method has optimal generalizability for all types of motion is a question worth exploring.
2. Potential for Error Propagation: The quality of the final output is critically dependent on the fidelity of the initial ACT-PAE encoding. The ACT-PAE is trained by the reconstruction loss. However, reconstructing the motion well does not guarantee that the resulting latent phase space is optimal for the downstream diffusion task. The authors should discuss this in the revison.

questions.value:
Though this work is quite interesting and the experiments seems to be promising, I have to stay "Borderline accept" currently. The authors should answer the following questions:
1. The ACT-PAE is the cornerstone of the entire framework. How does it perform on highly aperiodic, non-cyclic motions (e.g., stumbling, complex object interaction, modern dance)? Have you quantified its reconstruction error on such motions and compared it with more standard VAE-based autoencoders?

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel framework called Compositional Phase Diffusion for generating long motion sequences with smooth transitions and semantic alignment. The framework addresses the challenge of awkward transitions between motion segments in existing motion generation models by introducing two key modules: the Semantic Phase Diffusion Module (SPDM) and the Transitional Phase Diffusion Module (TPDM). These modules operate within the latent space of a pre-trained Action-Centric Motion Phase Autoencoder (ACT-PAE) to incorporate semantic guidance and phase details from adjacent motion clips during the diffusion process. The framework can handle an arbitrary number of motion segments of varying lengths simultaneously, ensuring smooth and coherent transitions between clips. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework through extensive experiments on tasks such as compositional motion generation and motion inbetweening. The experimental results show significant improvements in motion realism and contextual alignment, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods. The framework's flexibility and scalability are also highlighted, as it can accommodate various application scenarios.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths: 

1. The proposed Compositional Phase Diffusion framework introduces a novel approach to long-term motion generation by combining semantic guidance and phase dynamics information from adjacent motion segments. This effectively addresses the issue of awkward transitions between motion clips, which is a significant challenge in existing methods.

2. The paper presents comprehensive experimental evaluations on the BABEL-TEACH dataset, demonstrating the framework's superiority over other state-of-the-art methods in terms of motion realism (FID) and contextual alignment (MMD). For example, in compositional motion pair generation tasks, the proposed method achieves an overall FID score of 0.782 and an overall MMD score of 4.711, outperforming priorMDM, TEACH, and other methods.

3. The framework's ability to process multiple motion segments of varying lengths simultaneously is a notable advantage. This flexibility allows it to handle complex motion sequencing tasks and facilitates motion inbetweening tasks by denoising multiple motion segments in parallel.

4. The proposed framework provides a scalable solution for various motion generation tasks, including long-term compositional generation and motion inbetweening. By introducing the ACT-PAE, SPDM, and TPDM components, the framework offers new insights into motion phase modeling and diffusion-based motion generation, advancing the field of human motion synthesis.


Weaknesses: 

1. The paper relies on the BABEL-TEACH dataset for training and evaluation, which may limit the generalizability of the proposed method. The authors acknowledge that BABEL-TEACH is the only dataset providing subsequence pair annotations, but this could restrict the applicability of the framework to other motion datasets.

2. The paper proposes a phase mixing parameter r to balance semantic denoising and transitional denoising, but it does not thoroughly explore the impact of different r values on motion quality and transition smoothness. A more comprehensive ablation study on this parameter would strengthen the paper.

3. The paper primarily uses FID and MMD for evaluation, but these metrics may not fully capture the nuances of motion quality, particularly aspects like motion dynamics and physical plausibility. Incorporating additional metrics, such as joint velocity errors or root mean squared jerk, could provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

questions.value:
1. How would the proposed framework perform on other motion datasets, such as HumanML3D or AMASS? Are there any dataset-specific factors that might affect the framework's performance? How are the performances compared to recent motion generation methods like MoMask? 

2. How were the phase mixe parameter values determined? Could a learnable parameter or adaptive mechanism for r further improve motion quality and transition smoothness?

3. The motion inbetweening experiments focus on relatively short transition lengths (60-180 frames). How would the framework perform for longer inbetweening tasks, such as generating transitions spanning several seconds or more?

title.value: Deep Compositional Phase Diffusion for Long Motion Sequence Generation

TLDR.value: The proposed Compositional Phase Diffusion framework consistently generates semantically aligned multi-clip motion with smooth transitions by using latent-phase diffusion modules (SPDM and TPDM) to preserve phase continuity and enable inbetweening.

abstract.value:
Recent research on motion generation has shown significant progress in generating semantically aligned motion with singular semantics. However, when employing these models to create composite sequences containing multiple semantically generated motion clips, they often struggle to preserve the continuity of motion dynamics at the transition boundaries between clips, resulting in awkward transitions and abrupt artifacts. To address these challenges, we present Compositional Phase Diffusion, which leverages the Semantic Phase Diffusion Module (SPDM) and Transitional Phase Diffusion Module (TPDM) to progressively incorporate semantic guidance and phase details from adjacent motion clips into the diffusion process. Specifically, SPDM and TPDM operate within the latent motion frequency domain established by the pre-trained Action-Centric Motion Phase Autoencoder (ACT-PAE). This allows them to learn semantically important and transition-aware phase information from variable-length motion clips during training. Experimental results demonstrate the competitive performance of our proposed framework in generating compositional motion sequences that align semantically with the input conditions, while preserving phase transitional continuity between preceding and succeeding motion clips. Additionally, motion inbetweening task is made possible by keeping the phase parameter of the input motion sequences fixed throughout the diffusion process, showcasing the potential for extending the proposed framework to accommodate various application scenarios. Codes are available at
https://github.com/asdryau/TransPhase.
